newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR suspends work in Rwanda region after killing.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR suspends work in Rwanda region after killing.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency suspended work on Friday in a troubled Rwandan region full of returnees after a Hutu driver, his wife and two children were killed in the third attack against aid staff in just over a week.

Spokesman Fernando del Mundo said UNHCR evacuated local staff from the northwestern Ruhengeri region following the Thursday night killing of driver Felicien Bucyekabili and his family members in nearby Kigombe village.
"We have suspended our operations in Ruhengeri. We do monitoring (of refugees) essentially in Ruhengeri," he told a news briefing.

UNHCR and other international agency staff had already pulled out of the predominantly Hutu region on Zaire's frontier and other border areas of Rwanda after a series of brutal and unexplained murders of expatriate aid workers earlier this year.
Gunmen in Rwanda killed three Spanish relief workers in January and five U.N. human rights workers in February.
Because of insecurity, UNHCR expatriate staff had not been to Ruhengeri, which absorbed 300,000 Hutu returnees from Zaire since late last year, for the past two weeks, del Mundo said.
UNHCR was investigating the circumstances surrounding the killing. Its Rwanda country head Roman Urasa, accompanied by a government minister, was travelling to the region, he added.

Only last week, a Rwandan Hutu field officer working for the U.N. food agency was found dead in his home in Kigombe with his wife, small child and a relative. The body of another World Food Programme Hutu employee was found in a forest nearby on Tuesday.
Aid officials, who expressed alarm at the violence, said the latest killings coincided with a big operation by Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army in Ruhengeri.

"It's almost getting to the stage of pitched battles," said a senior aid official in Geneva who is following the region. "In addition, there seems to be individual acts of ethnically-motivated violence."
Ethnic tensions in Rwanda have risen sharply with the return of 800,000 Hutu refugees from Zaire since last year, who fled in fear of reprisal for 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis.
Many Tutsi survivors accuse the returnees of taking part in the slaughters and want an eye for an eye.
Among the Hutu returnees are militiamen who played a key role in the genocide and are now at odds with the army.
Amnesty International has accused Rwandan troops of unlawful executions of civilians in reprisal for attacks on government soldiers and then saying civilians were killed in cross-fire.
UNHCR, which has airlifted more than 50,000 Rwandan Hutus from Zaire to Kigali in recent months, says it has been unable to monitor the bulk of the returnees.
Aid agencies say 25 percent of Rwanda is completely out of bounds and 50 percent only accessible with an army escort.
